Shoshany, A C++17 thread pool for high-performance scientific computing, SoftwareX 26 (2024) 101687, arXiv:2105.00613. 1. Introduction Precision calculations for the LHC and for rare decays rest on multi-loop Feynman integrals. Once a process is computed beyond leading order, its diagrams are assembled into families of scalar integrals, and every family is reduced to a small set of master integrals with integration-by-parts (IBP) identities [7, 8, 9]. The masters are then evaluated analytically or numerically. Their number is finite [10], yet choosing a basis that keeps the coefficients small is a problem of its own [11, 12]. Typical applications include Higgs production at three loops [13], charged-current Drell–Yan production at N3 LO [14], two-loop five-point amplitudes [15], and the 2 → 3 reactions on the Les Houches precision wishlist [16]. The reduction is the common step, and recent reviews describe its algorithms and its cost [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. The standard Laporta algorithm [9] turns the reduction into the elimination of a finite system, and the size of that system sets the cost. An integral is characterized by its depth, the total power of the propagators in the denominator, and its rank, the total power of the numerator. The algorithm chooses two bounds, Dmax and Rmax, one layer above the largest depth and rank among the integrals to be reduced, and applies the identities to every integral with depth less than Dmax and rank less than Rmax. These integrals are the seeds. Integrals with the same set of propagators in the denominator form a sector.
